title: Agency and contract law
summary: Who a producer represents, the three kinds of authority, what makes a contract valid, and the doctrines courts use to read a policy.
objectives: Tell express, implied and apparent authority apart
Name the elements of a legal contract, with Michigan's rules
Recognize adhesion, aleatory, conditional, unilateral and personal contracts
Separate representation, warranty, concealment, fraud, waiver and estoppel

scenes.title: Agency and contract law
scenes.subtitle: Who the producer works for, and the legal rules inside every policy

beats.text: This lesson covers agency and contract law.
beats.say: This lesson covers agency and contract law.

beats.text: You'll learn who a producer represents, what makes a contract valid, and how courts read a policy.
beats.say: You'll learn who a producer represents, what makes a contract valid, and how courts read a policy.

items.label: Agent of the insurer
items.detail: Sells, solicits or negotiates as the insurer's representative

items.label: Agent of the insured
items.detail: Not appointed by the insurer writing the policy; represents the insured

items.label: A license is not authority
items.detail: A license alone creates no authority to commit an insurer

items.label: Fiduciary for premiums
items.detail: Premiums go in a separate account, apart from the agent's own money

beats.text: In Michigan, an agent of the insurer sells, solicits or negotiates as the insurer's representative.
beats.say: In Michigan, an agent of the insurer sells, solicits or negotiates as the insurer's representative.

beats.text: A producer not appointed by the insurer writing the policy is an agent of the insured, and represents the insured.
beats.say: A producer not appointed by the insurer writing the policy is an agent of the insured, and represents the insured.

beats.text: A license by itself creates no authority to commit an insurer.
beats.say: A license by itself creates no authority to commit an insurer.

beats.text: And an agent is a fiduciary for money received as agent: premiums go in a separate account, apart from the agent's own money.
beats.say: And an agent is a fiduciary for money received as agent: premiums go in a separate account, apart from the agent's own money.

scenes.title: Three kinds of authority
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: express authority; implied authority; apparent agency; Cornell LII Wex: express authority
scenes.hook: Express is Explained, Implied is Inferred, Apparent is how it Appears.
items: Express: spelled out by the insurer, orally or in writing
Implied: not stated, but reasonably necessary to do the granted job
Apparent: what a reasonable person would assume from the insurer's conduct

beats.text: Authority comes in three kinds. Express is Explained, Implied is Inferred, Apparent is how it Appears.
beats.say: Authority comes in three kinds. Express is Explained, Implied is Inferred, Apparent is how it Appears.

beats.text: Express authority is spelled out by the insurer, orally or in writing, like the powers in the agency contract.
beats.say: Express authority is spelled out by the insurer, orally or in writing, like the powers in the agency contract.

beats.text: Implied authority isn't stated, but it's reasonably necessary to do the job you were given.
beats.say: Implied authority isn't stated, but it's reasonably necessary to do the job you were given.

beats.text: Apparent authority is what a reasonable person would assume you have from the insurer's conduct. It's tied to estoppel.
beats.say: Apparent authority is what a reasonable person would assume you have from the insurer's conduct. It's tied to estoppel.

scenes.title: The agent who kept the binders
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: apparent agency; express authority; question core-012
scenes.story: An insurer ends an agent's binding authority but leaves him its signs and blank binder forms. A customer who reasonably believes he can still bind buys a binder from him.

items.label: What did the customer see?
items.detail: The insurer's signs and binder forms, left in place

items.label: Was the belief reasonable?
items.detail: Yes, based on the insurer's own conduct

scenes.answer: Apparent authority. The insurer may be estopped from denying it.

beats.text: Here's a story. An insurer ends an agent's binding authority but leaves him its signs and blank binders. A customer buys a binder. What authority is that?
beats.say: Here's a story. An insurer ends an agent's binding authority but leaves him its signs and blank binders. A customer buys a binder. What authority is that?

beats.text: Not express. The insurer withdrew it. But the customer saw the insurer's signs and forms, and reasonably believed he could bind.
beats.say: Not express. The insurer withdrew it. But the customer saw the insurer's signs and forms, and reasonably believed he could bind.

beats.text: That's apparent authority. Because of its own conduct, the insurer may be estopped from denying it.
beats.say: That's apparent authority. Because of its own conduct, the insurer may be estopped from denying it.

scenes.q: An agent's contract lets her sell auto policies but never mentions giving customers ID cards, a step reasonably necessary to complete the sale. Her authority to hand out ID cards is:
scenes.why: It isn't spelled out, so it isn't express. It's reasonably necessary to do the job she was given, so it's implied.

beats.text: Your turn. An agent may sell auto policies, but her contract never mentions handing out ID cards, a step she needs to finish the sale. What authority covers the ID cards? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Your turn. An agent may sell auto policies, but her contract never mentions handing out ID cards, a step she needs to finish the sale. What authority covers the ID cards? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: Implied authority. It isn't written down, but it's reasonably necessary to carry out what she was expressly allowed to do.
reveal.say: Implied authority. It isn't written down, but it's reasonably necessary to carry out what she was expressly allowed to do.

scenes.title: Elements of a legal contract
scenes.src: AFT Michigan v Michigan (2015); Gorham v Peerless Life (1962); MCL 722.52(1); ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Agreement
scenes.hook: Our Agent Collects Cash Legally: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration, Competent parties, Legal purpose.
items: Offer and acceptance: the application offers; a policy or binder accepts
Consideration: premium plus compliance, for the insurer's promise to pay
Competent parties: legal age and mental capacity; 18 in Michigan
Legal purpose: contracts for acts a statute prohibits are void or unenforceable

beats.text: Now, contracts. Our Agent Collects Cash Legally: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration, Competent parties, Legal purpose.
beats.say: Now, contracts. Our Agent Collects Cash Legally: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration, Competent parties, Legal purpose.

beats.text: In Michigan, the application is a mere offer, and the insurer's silence generally isn't acceptance. The insurer accepts by issuing the policy or a binder.
beats.say: In Michigan, the application is a mere offer, and the insurer's silence generally isn't acceptance. The insurer accepts by issuing the policy or a binder.

beats.text: The insured's consideration is the premium plus compliance with the policy. The insurer's is its promise to pay. Don't flip them.
beats.say: The insured's consideration is the premium plus compliance with the policy. The insurer's is its promise to pay. Don't flip them.

beats.text: Competent parties have legal age and the mental capacity to understand the contract. In Michigan, legal age is 18.
beats.say: Competent parties have legal age and the mental capacity to understand the contract. In Michigan, legal age is eighteen.

beats.text: And the purpose must be legal. A policy insuring a shipment of illegal drugs is unenforceable.
beats.say: And the purpose must be legal. A policy insuring a shipment of illegal drugs is unenforceable.

scenes.title: What makes insurance contracts different
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: adhesion; aleatory; unilateral; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. C; Secs. I and II Cond. E
scenes.hook: Every policy is served in A CUP, A: Adhesion, Conditional, Unilateral, Personal, Aleatory.
items: Adhesion: the insurer drafts it; take it or leave it
Conditional: payment depends on the insured meeting conditions
Unilateral: only the insurer promises. Personal: no assignment without consent
Aleatory: an unequal exchange that depends on an uncertain event

beats.text: Insurance contracts have five traits. Every policy is served in A CUP, A.
beats.say: Insurance contracts have five traits. Every policy is served in A CUP, A.

beats.text: Adhesion: the insurer drafts it; you take it or leave it. So ambiguities are read against the insurer.
beats.say: Adhesion: the insurer drafts it; you take it or leave it. So ambiguities are read against the insurer.

beats.text: Conditional: the insurer's duty to pay depends on you meeting conditions, like your duties after a loss.
beats.say: Conditional: the insurer's duty to pay depends on you meeting conditions, like your duties after a loss.

beats.text: Unilateral: only the insurer makes enforceable promises. Personal: it insures you, not the property, so assignment needs the insurer's written consent.
beats.say: Unilateral: only the insurer makes enforceable promises. Personal: it insures you, not the property, so assignment needs the insurer's written consent.

beats.text: Aleatory: an unequal exchange that depends on an uncertain event. Don't confuse it with adhesion, which is about who wrote it.
beats.say: Aleatory: an unequal exchange that depends on an uncertain event. Don't confuse it with adhesion, which is about who wrote it.

scenes.q: One insured pays premiums for ten years and never has a claim. Another pays for one month and collects a large loss. This unequal exchange shows that an insurance policy is:
scenes.why: Aleatory means an unequal exchange of value that depends on an uncertain event. Adhesion is about who drafted the policy.

beats.text: Check the two A's. One insured pays premiums for ten years with no claim. Another pays for one month and collects a large loss. Which trait is that? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Check the two A's. One insured pays premiums for ten years with no claim. Another pays for one month and collects a large loss. Which trait is that? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: Aleatory. The exchange is unequal and depends on an uncertain event. Adhesion would be about who drafted the policy.
reveal.say: Aleatory. The exchange is unequal and depends on an uncertain event. Adhesion would be about who drafted the policy.

scenes.title: How courts read a policy
scenes.src: IRMI glossary; Wilkie v Auto-Owners Ins Co, 469 Mich 41 (2003); National Alliance glossary: indemnity

items.label: Ambiguities
items.detail: Construed against the insurer, the drafter

items.label: Reasonable expectations
items.detail: Some courts give the coverage an insured would reasonably expect. Michigan declined it

items.label: Indemnity
items.detail: Restore the insured to the pre-loss position, without profit

items.label: Utmost good faith
items.detail: Both parties presumed to disclose all pertinent facts

beats.text: Courts read policies with a few rules. Ambiguous wording is construed against the insurer, which drafted it.
beats.say: Courts read policies with a few rules. Ambiguous wording is construed against the insurer, which drafted it.

beats.text: Some courts apply the reasonable expectations doctrine, giving the coverage an insured would reasonably expect. Michigan declined to adopt it, but that's still its name.
beats.say: Some courts apply the reasonable expectations doctrine, giving the coverage an insured would reasonably expect. Michigan declined to adopt it, but that's still its name.

beats.text: Indemnity restores you to your position before the loss, without profit. Even with two policies, you can't collect more than the loss.
beats.say: Indemnity restores you to your position before the loss, without profit. Even with two policies, you can't collect more than the loss.

beats.text: And utmost good faith presumes both parties disclose all pertinent facts.
beats.say: And utmost good faith presumes both parties disclose all pertinent facts.

scenes.title: Four voices on an application
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: representation; warranty; concealment; fraud; MCL 500.2218(1), (2)
scenes.hook: Four voices on an application: 'To the best of my knowledge' (representation). 'I guarantee it' (warranty). 'You didn't ask' (concealment). 'Gotcha' (fraud).
items: Representation: believed true. In Michigan, a false one voids only if material
Warranty: guaranteed true; voids the policy if untrue
Concealment: willfully withholding facts the insurer didn't ask about
Fraud: intent to deceive, unlike an innocent misstatement

beats.text: Picture four voices on an application. To the best of my knowledge. I guarantee it. You didn't ask. Gotcha.
beats.say: Picture four voices on an application. To the best of my knowledge. I guarantee it. You didn't ask. Gotcha.

beats.text: A representation is believed true. In Michigan, a misrepresentation voids the policy only if it's material: the insurer would have refused the contract had it known.
beats.say: A representation is believed true. In Michigan, a misrepresentation voids the policy only if it's material: the insurer would have refused the contract had it known.

beats.text: A warranty is guaranteed true, and it voids the policy if it's untrue.
beats.say: A warranty is guaranteed true, and it voids the policy if it's untrue.

beats.text: Concealment is willfully holding back pertinent facts, even when the insurer didn't ask. Fraud means intent to deceive.
beats.say: Concealment is willfully holding back pertinent facts, even when the insurer didn't ask. Fraud means intent to deceive.

scenes.q: An applicant knows his basement floods every spring but says nothing, because the application never asks about water. This is:
scenes.why: Concealment is willfully holding back pertinent information even though the insurer did not ask. It can void the policy.

beats.text: Try this. An applicant knows his basement floods every spring, but says nothing because the application never asks about water. What is that? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Try this. An applicant knows his basement floods every spring, but says nothing because the application never asks about water. What is that? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: Concealment. He willfully held back a pertinent fact he wasn't asked about, and that can void the policy.
reveal.say: Concealment. He willfully held back a pertinent fact he wasn't asked about, and that can void the policy.

scenes.title: Waiver vs. estoppel
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: waiver; estoppel; ISO HO 00 03 05 11 (2011 homeowners), Secs. I and II Cond. B
scenes.hook: Waiver: you WAVE goodbye to a right on purpose. Estoppel: the law says STOP, you can't go back on conduct someone reasonably relied on.
items: Waiver: the intentional, voluntary surrender of a known right
Estoppel: can't contradict earlier conduct someone reasonably relied on
An insurer that kept accepting late premiums may be estopped from canceling
2011 homeowners form: a waiver must be in writing by the insurer

beats.text: Last pair. Waiver: you wave goodbye to a right on purpose. Estoppel: the law says stop, you can't go back on conduct someone reasonably relied on.
beats.say: Last pair. Waiver: you wave goodbye to a right on purpose. Estoppel: the law says stop, you can't go back on conduct someone reasonably relied on.

beats.text: If an insurer keeps accepting late premiums, it may be estopped from canceling for late payment.
beats.say: If an insurer keeps accepting late premiums, it may be estopped from canceling for late payment.

beats.text: Policies limit casual waivers. The 2011 homeowners form requires a waiver to be in writing by the insurer.
beats.say: Policies limit casual waivers. The twenty eleven homeowners form requires a waiver to be in writing by the insurer.

items: Michigan: not appointed by the insurer writing it? Insured's agent
Express is explained, implied inferred, apparent how it appears
Offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties, legal purpose
A CUP, A: adhesion, conditional, unilateral, personal, aleatory
A warranty is guaranteed; concealment is silence on purpose

beats.text: In Michigan, a producer not appointed by the insurer writing the policy represents the insured. Express is explained, implied inferred, apparent appears.
beats.say: In Michigan, a producer not appointed by the insurer writing the policy represents the insured. Express is explained, implied inferred, apparent appears.

beats.text: Contracts need offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties and legal purpose. Policies come in A CUP, A. A warranty is guaranteed; concealment is silence on purpose.
beats.say: Contracts need offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties and legal purpose. Policies come in A CUP, A. A warranty is guaranteed; concealment is silence on purpose.
